title: The Address
blurb: You arrive alone in a strange city at night, with one letter and one night to find the address on it.

text.B1:
So you tell her all of it. The station at eleven, the number nine bus, the dust on the window, the man at number 16 in his dressing gown. She listens to every word without interrupting once. When you finish she sits back and says: "Most people would have gone home last night. When can you start?"

You start on Monday. The first job they give you is fixing the letters.
text.B2:
So you tell her all of it. The station at eleven at night, the number nine bus, the dust on the inside of the window. The man at number 16 who answered the door in a dressing gown and told you the truth anyway. She listens to every word of it without once interrupting, which is not a thing you are used to. When you finish she sits back and says, "Most people would have gone home last night. When can you start?"

text.A2:
There is no job today. But she takes your name and your number. She writes them on real paper, not on a screen. "We will have something in the spring," she says. "Call me. And use this address, not the old one."

text.B1:
There is no job for you today. But she takes your name and number, and writes them on a real piece of paper rather than typing them into a screen. You decide to take that as a good sign. "We will have something in the spring," she says. "Call me then. And use this address, not the one on your letter."

text.B2:
There is no job for you today, and she does not pretend otherwise. But she takes your name and your number and writes them on an actual piece of paper rather than typing them into a screen. You decide, on no evidence at all, to take that as a good sign. "We will have something in the spring. Call me then — and use this address, not the one printed on your letter."

It is not what you came for. But you are in the city now, and somebody in it knows your name.

nodes.note: The most common ending. Deliberately not a failure — a first day in a city rarely is.

text.A2:
"Ms Rowe?" you say.

She stops with her key in the door and turns round. Nobody has told you her name. Nobody at Mill Quay knows you are coming. She looks at you for a long moment, and then she starts to smile.

"You went to Rosewater Street," she says. "Didn't you."

You start on Monday. She tells everybody this story for years.
text.B1:
"Ms Rowe?"

She stops with her key halfway to the door and turns round. Nobody at Mill Quay knows you are coming; nobody here has told you her name. She looks at you for a long moment, working it out, and then she begins to smile.

"You went to Rosewater Street," she says. "Didn't you."

text.B2:
"Ms Rowe?"

She stops with her key halfway to the lock and turns round. Nobody at Mill Quay knows you are coming, and nobody at Mill Quay has told you her name, which means there is exactly one place you can have got it from. You can see her arriving at that conclusion in real time, and you can see the precise moment she decides she likes it.

"You went to Rosewater Street," she says. "Didn't you."

You start on Monday. She tells this story to new arrivals for years afterwards, and it improves every time.

The number rings and rings. Then it stops working. You go back to the agency at lunchtime. The yellow sign is still there. The door is locked. Inside, there is nobody at all.

text.B1:
The number rings and rings, and then it stops connecting at all. You go back to the agency at lunchtime. The yellow sign is still up and the door is locked. Through the glass you can see that the bright, warm office has no furniture in it at all.

text.B2:
The number rings and rings, and then, at some point that afternoon, it stops connecting altogether. You go back at lunchtime. You have no money, no job, and a receipt with a dead telephone number on it. It is not yet noon on your first full day.

You sit in the station and watch the departure board. There is a train at two o'clock going back the way you came, and you have just about enough money for a ticket.

Somewhere in this city, a woman with your name in her diary waits until half past nine. Then she decides you are not coming, and goes back to work.
text.B2:
You sit in the station and watch the departure board turn over. There is a train at two o'clock going back the way you came, and you have, just about, enough money for a ticket to be on it.

Somewhere in this city, a woman with your name written in her diary waits until half past nine, decides that you are not coming after all, and goes back to work. She does not think about it again. You will think about it for a long time.

text.B1: Name, number, reference. Everything goes smoothly, and by lunchtime you have the job. Nobody asks how you got here, or what the night cost you, and you do not say. You got exactly what you came for. Standing on the new carpet, you wait to feel something, and nothing comes.

text.B1: You reach Mill Quay at twenty past nine. The diary is closed, the chairs in reception are full of other people, and the woman behind the desk is kind and completely final. "Try us in the spring," she says, and you both know she means no. Outside, the river goes on exactly as before.
text.B2: You reach Mill Quay at twenty past nine. The diary is closed, the chairs in reception are full of other, punctual people, and the woman behind the desk is kind and entirely final about it. text.A2: The morning is grey over the bench, and you let it come. You are too cold and too tired to move. Just a minute, you tell yourself. But by the time you can feel your feet, nine o'clock has gone. And so has the reason you came.
text.B1: The morning comes up grey over the station bench, and you let it. You are too cold and too tired to move. It is only for a minute, you tell yourself. But by the time you can feel your feet, nine o'clock has gone — and so has the reason you came.
text.B2: The morning comes up grey over the station bench, and you let it come. You are too cold and too spent to move, and you tell yourself it is only for a minute more. But by the time the feeling has crept back into your feet, nine o'clock has been and gone — and gone with it is the single reason you came to this city at all.

text.A2: You take a wrong turn, then another. The same closed shop goes past twice. The map means nothing now. The streets are very quiet. At one in the morning, the city belongs to no one.

text.B2: You take a wrong turning, and then another, until the same shuttered shop has slid past you twice and the map in your hand has ceased to mean anything at all. text.B2: Go to the job address the agency gave you.

text.B1: On the reception desk there is a tray of returned post — old letters, each with the Rosewater Street address crossed out by hand. You look again. One of them, you realise slowly, is your own: the letter that brought you across a country to the wrong door.
text.B2: On the reception desk stands a tray of returned post — old letters, each with the Rosewater Street address struck out by hand. You look again, and then again, and the recognition arrives slowly and coldly. One of them is unmistakably your own: the very letter that carried you the length of a country to a door that no longer opens.

text.A2: Mention the letters to the receptionist.
text.B1: Mention the letters to the receptionist.
text.B2: Mention the letters to the receptionist.

text.A2: Say nothing about it.
text.B1: Say nothing about it.
text.B2: Say nothing about it.

text.A2: The driver tells the story as he drives. "They all moved to the river. Glass offices, very smart." He looks at you in the mirror. "And watch the work agencies near the station. They are not what they seem."
text.B1: The driver settles into the story as he drives. "They all moved to the river. Glass offices, very smart." He catches your eye in the mirror. "And watch the work agencies near the station. They are not what they look like. Not for people like you."
text.B2: The driver settles comfortably into the story as he drives. "They all moved down to the river. Glass offices, very smart, very modern." He finds your eyes in the mirror. "And you want to watch those work agencies near the station. They are not what they appear to be — not for people newly arrived, people like you."

text.A2: Ask him to take you to Rosewater Street.
text.B1: Ask him to take you to Rosewater Street.
text.B2: Ask him to take you to Rosewater Street.

text.A2: Ask for a cheap hotel near the water.

text.B2: Ask for a cheap hotel near the water.

text.A2: First light is grey over Mill Quay. A coffee cart is opening. Vans go by along the water. You are early, and you are clean. For the first time, you know where you are, and where to go.
text.B1: First light comes up grey over Mill Quay. A coffee cart is opening; delivery vans hum along the water. You are early, and you are clean. For the first time since the train, you know where you are, and where you are going.
text.B2: First light comes up grey and even over Mill Quay. A coffee cart is cranking open its shutter; delivery vans hum along the water. You are early, and you are clean, and for the first time since you stepped off that train you know with real precision both where you are and where you are going.

text.A2: Buy a coffee, and go in to reception.
text.B1: Buy a coffee, and go in to reception.
text.B2: Buy a coffee, and go in to reception.

text.A2: Wait by the water, and watch the door.

text.B2: Wait by the water, and watch the door.

text.B2: Overhear the coffee-cart queue.

text.A2: You watch the doors along the quay. Then you see him: the man in the good suit from the agency. He goes into a building two doors down. No sign, no name. The way he looks around first tells you everything.
text.B1: Watching the other doors along the quay, you see him: the man in the good suit from the agency. He lets himself into a building two doors down. There is no sign on it, and no name. Something about the way he looks around first tells you everything.
text.B2: Watching the other doors strung along the quay, you catch sight of him: the man in the good suit from the agency, letting himself into a building two doors down. There is no sign on it and no name of any kind, and something in the careful, sidelong way he checks the street before he enters tells you everything you needed to know.

text.A2: Go in to reception now, certain of things.
text.B1: Go in to reception now, certain of things.
text.B2: Go in to reception now, certain of things.

text.B1: Keep to the water until nine.
text.B2: Keep to the water until nine.

text.A2: Let him see that you saw him.

text.A2: In your bag: the letter, a little money, and a photo you do not take out. You read the letter again. You know every word. It is as if the words might change while you sleep.
text.B1: In your bag there is the letter, a little money that will not last long, and a photograph you do not take out. You read the letter again, though you know every word by heart. It is as if the words might have changed while you slept.
text.B2: In your bag there is the letter, a little money that will plainly not stretch far, and a photograph you deliberately do not take out. You read the letter once more, though you have long since known it by heart, half persuaded that the words might have quietly altered themselves while you slept in your seat.

text.A2: Go and ask at the information desk.
text.B1: Go and ask at the information desk.
text.B2: Go and ask at the information desk.

text.A2: Go out into the night.
text.B1: Go out into the night.
text.B2: Go out into the night.

text.B1: Your phone has one bar of battery left. One. You could use it now to look up the firm and settle the question, or save it for something worse later on. In a strange city at night, a dying phone is a kind of clock, counting down.
text.B2: Your phone shows a single bar of battery — one — and the choice it forces is oddly stark. You might use it now to look up the firm and settle the question outright, or hoard it against some worse moment still to come. In a strange city after midnight, a dying phone becomes a kind of clock, counting down to a silence you would rather not meet.

text.A2: Use the last of it to search the firm.
text.B1: Use the last of it to search the firm.
text.B2: Use the last of it to search the firm.

text.A2: Save it, and ask people instead.
text.B1: Save it, and ask people instead.
text.B2: Save it, and ask people instead.

text.A2: An old page loads, slowly. The firm's address is not Rosewater Street. It is somewhere by the river. Then the screen goes black and stays black. You are alone again with a paper letter.
text.B1: An old page loads, slowly. The firm's address is not Rosewater Street at all, but somewhere down on the river. Then the screen goes black and stays black, and you are alone again with a paper letter and whatever you can remember.
text.B2: An old page loads, grudgingly and by degrees. The firm's registered address, it turns out, is not Rosewater Street at all, but somewhere down along the river. Then the screen blinks to black and stays black, and you are returned to your own devices — a paper letter, and whatever you can hold in your head.

text.A2: Take the bus — you know it is the river now.
text.B1: Take the bus — you know it is the river now.
text.B2: Take the bus — you know it is the river now.

text.A2: Walk, now that you know where.
text.B1: Walk, now that you know where.
text.B2: Walk, now that you know where.

text.A2: Mara has more sense than money. You have a little more money than sense. Together, it might be enough to do this well. If not, you will both walk the wrong way half the night.
text.B1: Mara has more sense than money, and you have a little more money than sense. Between you there might be just enough to do this properly. Otherwise you will both walk half the night the wrong way, too proud to say you are lost.
text.B2: Mara, you gather, has rather more sense than money, while you have marginally more money than sense. Between the two of you there might just be enough to manage this properly. The alternative is both of you tramping half the night in the wrong direction, each too proud to be the first to admit to being lost.

text.A2: Share a taxi, and drop Mara off first.
text.B1: Share a taxi, and drop Mara off first.
text.B2: Share a taxi, and drop Mara off first.

text.A2: Take the bus together.
text.B1: Take the bus together.
text.B2: Take the bus together.

text.A2: A guard walks the hall, turning off lights. "We're closing. You can't sit here." He is not unkind, just tired. Behind him the big hall goes dark, piece by piece. The cold comes in.
text.B1: A guard walks the concourse, turning off the lights one bank at a time. "Station's closing. You can't sit here." He is not unkind, only tired, and he means it. Behind him the big hall goes dark in pieces, and the cold comes in.
text.B2: A guard works his way along the concourse, killing the lights a bank at a time. "Station's closing. You can't sit about here." There is no unkindness in it, only fatigue, and he plainly means it. Behind him the great hall goes dark in sections, and with each one the cold presses a little further in.

text.A2: Move on, out into the night.
text.B1: Move on, out into the night.
text.B2: Move on, out into the night.

text.A2: Ask him the way before you go.
text.B1: Ask him the way before you go.
text.B2: Ask him the way before you go.

text.A2: From the bus window the city goes by, dark and wet and strange. You could get off early and walk. Or you could stay on to the right stop, and trust the driver to know the way.
text.B1: From the bus window the city slides past, dark and wet and unfamiliar. You could get off early and find your own feet. Or you could stay on to the proper stop, and trust the driver to know his route better than you.
text.B2: From the bus window the city unspools past you, dark and wet and wholly unfamiliar. You could get down early and trust your own two feet. Or you could stay aboard to the proper stop, and trust instead that the driver knows his route rather better than a stranger with a useless map.

text.A2: Get off early and walk the last part.
text.B1: Get off early and walk the last part.
text.B2: Get off early and walk the last part.

text.A2: Stay on to the Rosewater stop.
text.B1: Stay on to the Rosewater stop.
text.B2: Stay on to the Rosewater stop.

text.A2: Reception is warm. It smells of coffee. The woman at the desk is kind. She looks at you a little too long. Last night is all over you — the creased coat, the tired eyes. She says nothing.
text.B1: Reception is warm and smells of coffee. The woman behind the desk is kind, and she looks at you a moment longer than she needs to. Last night is written all over you — the creased coat, the tired eyes — and she reads it without a word.
text.B2: Reception is warm and smells faintly of coffee. The woman behind the desk is kind, and she holds your gaze a moment longer than strictly necessary. Last night is written all over you — the creased coat, the shadowed eyes, the particular stillness of the very tired — and she reads every line of it without a word.

text.A2: Ask to see Ms Rowe.
text.B1: Ask to see Ms Rowe.
text.B2: Ask whether you can see Ms Rowe.

text.A2: Leave your name and go.
text.B1: Leave your details and go.
text.B2: Leave your details and step back out.

text.A2: Talk to the person waiting with you.
text.B1: Talk to the candidate waiting beside you.
text.B2: Strike up a word with the candidate beside you.

text.A2: Ms Rowe's office looks over the water. On the desk is a folder. On top of it is a letter you know. It is yours — sent to the wrong street, and back again. She sees you see it.
text.B1: Ms Rowe's office looks out over the water. On the desk is a folder, and on top of the folder is a letter you recognise. It is your own — sent to the wrong street, and come back here again. She sees you see it, and says nothing yet.
text.B2: Ms Rowe's office gives onto the water. On the desk sits a folder, and squared on top of the folder is a letter you recognise at once: your own, sent to the wrong street, returned, and somehow arrived here ahead of you. She watches you take it in, and for the moment says nothing at all.

text.A2: Ask about the letter on the desk.
text.B1: Ask about the letter on the desk.
text.B2: Ask her about the letter squared on the desk.

text.A2: Talk about yourself instead.
text.B1: Talk about yourself instead.
text.B2: Turn the talk to yourself instead.

text.A2: Look out at the river.
text.B1: Look out at the river.
text.B2: Look out at the river a moment.

text.A2: "Someone here posted the old address for two years," she says. She turns the letter over. "You are not the first it sent the wrong way. You are the first to come anyway."
text.B1: "Someone here has been posting the old address for two years," she says, turning the returned letter over. "You are not the first it sent the wrong way. You are the first to arrive anyway."
text.B2: "Someone in this office has been posting the old address for two years," she says, turning the returned letter over in her fingers. "You are by no means the first it has sent astray." She sets it down and looks at you properly. "You are, however, the first to have come anyway."

text.A2: Offer to be the one who fixes the letters.
text.B1: Offer to be the one who fixes the letters.
text.B2: Offer to be the one who fixes the letters.

text.A2: Just say you found them, anyway.
text.B1: Just say you found them, anyway.
text.B2: Just say you found them, anyway.

text.A2: Ask who sends the old address.
text.B1: Ask who keeps sending the old address.
text.B2: Ask who has been sending the old address.

text.A2: She reaches the step with a coffee and keys. She sees you waiting. She is not surprised. "You look like you've been up all night," she says, and unlocks the door. "Come in, before we freeze."
text.B1: She reaches the step with a coffee in one hand and keys in the other, and sees you waiting there. She does not seem surprised. "You look like someone who has been up all night," she says, unlocking the door. "Come in, before we both freeze."
text.B2: She arrives at the step with a coffee in one hand and a bunch of keys in the other, and takes you in without the least surprise. "You have the look of someone who has been up the whole night," she says, fitting a key to the lock. "Come in, for pity's sake, before the pair of us freeze to the pavement."

text.A2: Help her with the door, and walk in together.
text.B1: Help her with the door, and walk in together.
text.B2: Help her with the door, and walk in together.

text.A2: Hang back, suddenly unsure.
text.B1: Hang back, suddenly unsure.
text.B2: Hang back, suddenly unsure.

text.A2: The quay is waking up: gulls on grey water, a coffee cart, vans on the stone. You have time, for once. Your hands are clean, for once. After such a night, it is strange to be early.
text.B1: The quay is waking around you: gulls on the grey water, a coffee cart, delivery vans humming along the stone. You have time, for once, and clean hands, for once. It is a strange thing, after such a night, to be simply early.
text.B2: The quay is stirring awake around you: gulls riding the grey water, a coffee cart, delivery vans humming along the worn stone. You have time, for once, and clean hands, for once. After a night like the one behind you, there is something almost disorienting in the simple fact of being early.

text.A2: Walk the quay a while to steady your nerves.
text.B1: Walk the quay a while to steady your nerves.
text.B2: Walk the quay a while to steady your nerves.

text.A2: Go straight in to reception.
text.B1: Go straight in to reception.
text.B2: Go straight in to reception.

text.A2: The man in the good suit sees you looking. For a second, neither of you moves. Then he goes into the building with no name, and is gone. Now you know what kind of place you left.
text.B1: The man in the good suit from the agency sees you seeing him. For a second neither of you moves. Then he lets himself into the unmarked building and is gone. You understand, standing there, exactly what kind of place you walked out of.
text.B2: The man in the good suit from the agency catches you watching him. For the length of a breath neither of you so much as moves. Then he lets himself into the unmarked building and is gone — and standing there in the cold morning, you understand with perfect clarity exactly what kind of place it was that you walked out of.

text.A2: Go in to reception before he can.
text.B1: Go in to reception before he can.
text.B2: Go in to reception before he can.

text.A2: Look away, and keep to the water.
text.B1: Look away, and keep to the water.
text.B2: Look away, and keep to the water.

text.A2: "They wanted money from me too," the other person says quietly. "To register, they said. I nearly paid." She shakes her head. So you are not the only one. That helps, a little.
text.B1: "They wanted money off me too," the other candidate says quietly. "For registration, they called it. I nearly paid." She shakes her head at herself. You are not the only one, then. That is worth something, though you could not say quite what.
text.B2: "They wanted money off me too," the other candidate murmurs. "For registration, they called it. I very nearly paid." She shakes her head at her own near miss. So you were not the only one, then — a small, cold comfort, and worth something all the same, though you could not easily put into words quite what.

text.A2: Take the warning to heart.
text.B1: Take the warning to heart.
text.B2: Take the warning to heart.

text.A2: Keep to yourself, and wait.
text.B1: Keep to yourself, and wait.
text.B2: Keep to yourself, and wait.

text.A2: Through the window you see the bridge you crossed in the dark. The black water under it is grey now. It does not look far by daylight. Most things do not, you are learning.
text.B1: Through the window you can see the bridge you crossed in the dark. The black water under it is ordinary and grey now. It does not look far at all by daylight. Most things do not, you are learning, by daylight.
text.B2: Through the window you can pick out the bridge you crossed in the dark, and the black water beneath it, entirely ordinary and grey now in the flat morning light. It does not look remotely far by daylight. Very little does, you are beginning to understand, once the daylight has got at it.

text.A2: Look closer at the folder and the letter.
text.B1: Look closer at the folder and the letter.
text.B2: Look closer at the folder and the letter.

text.A2: Keep your eyes on Ms Rowe.
text.B1: Keep your eyes on Ms Rowe.
text.B2: Keep your eyes on Ms Rowe.

text.A2: She calls a younger worker in. He goes red. "The old letterhead," she says, kindly. "We'll fix it." Then she looks at you. "And you can help us fix it. You know the way better than we do."
text.B1: She calls in a younger colleague, who goes red to the ears. "The old letterhead," she says, not unkindly. "We'll sort it." Then she turns back to you. "And you can help us sort it. You clearly know the way better than we do."
text.B2: She calls in a younger colleague, who colours to the roots of his hair. "The old letterhead," she says, not unkindly. "We shall sort it out." Then she turns back to you, and there is something decided in her face. "And you can help us sort it out. You clearly know the way to us rather better than we do ourselves."

text.A2: Offer to fix the letters yourself.
text.B1: Offer to fix the letters yourself.
text.B2: Offer to be the one who fixes the letters.

text.A2: Say nothing, and talk about the job.
text.B1: Let it drop, and talk about the job.
text.B2: Let the matter drop, and turn to the job.

text.A2: The kiosk woman calls after you. "There's a back way into number 14, through the yard. The front door hasn't opened in years." She points with her chin and turns for home.
text.B1: The kiosk woman calls after you, pulling the shutter the last of the way down. "There's a back way into number 14, through the yard. The front door hasn't opened in years." She points with her chin, already turning for home.
text.B2: The kiosk woman calls after you as she hauls the shutter down the last foot to the ground. "There's a back way into number 14, mind — through the yard. That front door's not opened in years." She tips her chin towards it, already turning for home and whatever warmth is waiting there.

text.A2: Go round the back, into the yard.
text.B1: Go round the back, into the yard.
text.B2: Go round the back, into the yard.

text.A2: Try the front of the building.
text.B1: Try the front of the building.
text.B2: Try the front of the building.

text.A2: In the yard, a low window is lit. Inside, on a desk, is a tray of envelopes, stamped and ready. You look closer, and go cold. Every one has the Rosewater Street address. To here. To no one.
text.B1: In the yard a low window is lit. Inside, on a desk, there is a tray of envelopes, stamped and ready to post. You lean closer, and the cold goes through you: every one of them is addressed to Rosewater Street. To here. To no one at all.
text.B2: In the yard a low window is lit, and inside, laid out on a desk, is a tray of envelopes, stamped and squared and ready for the post. You lean in closer, and the cold goes clean through you: every last one of them is addressed to Rosewater Street. To here. To no one who has worked here in two years.

text.A2: Look in the front window too.
text.B1: Look in the front window too.
text.B2: Look in the front window too.

text.A2: Come back at nine, when someone is here.
text.B1: Come back at nine, when someone is here.
text.B2: Come back at nine, when someone is here.

text.A2: The upstairs window opens. The girl leans out. "They're by the river now," she says, as if you should know. "Ada Rowe. My dad worked for her, before all this."
text.B1: Before you go, the upstairs window opens and the girl leans out into the cold. "They're by the river now," she says, matter-of-fact, as if you should have known. "Ada Rowe. My dad used to work for her, before all this."
text.B2: Before you can turn away, the upstairs window opens and the girl leans out into the cold air. "They're by the river now," she says, matter-of-factly, as though it were common knowledge you ought to have arrived with. "Ada Rowe. My dad used to work for her, before all of this went the way it did."

text.A2: Ask her more.
text.B1: Ask her more.
text.B2: Ask her more.

text.A2: Thank her, and wait for morning.
text.B1: Thank her, and wait for morning.
text.B2: Thank her, and wait for morning.

text.A2: "Three Mill Quay," she says, as if everyone knows. "Take the number four in the morning. It stops outside." Then her father calls her in. The window shuts. The street is yours again.
text.B1: "Three Mill Quay," she says, as if everyone knows it. "Take the number four in the morning. It stops right outside." Then her father's voice calls her back inside. The window shuts, and the street is yours again.
text.B2: "Three Mill Quay," she says, as if it were the most self-evident thing in the world. "Take the number four in the morning; it stops directly outside." Then her father's voice summons her back from somewhere inside. The window closes, and the street is handed back to you and the cold.

text.A2: Set off for the river.
text.B1: Set off for the river.
text.B2: Set off for the river.

text.A2: Find the café she mentioned.
text.B1: Find the café she mentioned.
text.B2: Find the café she mentioned.

text.A2: By the water, you lose the streets completely. But a boathouse has its lights on. You hear long oars carried down to the river, and low voices — people with somewhere to be.
text.B1: By the water you lose the thread of the streets entirely. But a boathouse has its lights on, early. You can hear long oars being carried down to the river. There are low voices too — people with somewhere to be.
text.B2: Down by the water you lose the thread of the streets entirely. But a boathouse has its lights burning, early, and there comes the hollow knock of long oars being carried down to the river. Low voices come with it — the unremarkable sounds of people who know precisely where they are going and why.

text.A2: Ask the rowers the way.
text.B1: Ask the rowers the way.
text.B2: Ask the rowers the way.

text.A2: Push on along the dark bank.
text.B1: Push on along the dark bank.
text.B2: Push on along the dark bank.

text.A2: "Mill Quay? Straight on, past the second bridge. Ten minutes." The rower does not stop, an oar on his shoulder. "You're nearly there," he says, seeing your face. "Nearly there now."
text.B1: "Mill Quay? Straight along, past the second bridge. Ten minutes." The rower barely breaks step, an oar balanced on one shoulder. "You're nearly there," he adds, seeing your face. "Whatever it is, you're nearly there now."
text.B2: "Mill Quay? Straight along the bank, past the second bridge. Ten minutes, no more." The rower scarcely breaks his stride, an oar balanced across one shoulder. "You're nearly there," he adds, catching something in your face, "whatever it is you're chasing. You're nearly there now."

text.A2: Follow the bank to the quay.
text.B1: Follow the bank to the quay.
text.B2: Follow the bank to the quay.

text.A2: Find the coffee cart and wait for nine.
text.B1: Find the coffee cart and wait for nine.
text.B2: Find the coffee cart and wait for nine.

text.A2: The new building has a glass hall, lit and empty. A guard's cap sits on an empty desk. Everything here is two years newer than your letter. You stand outside in last night's clothes.
text.B1: The new development has a glass lobby, lit and empty, a guard's cap left on an untended desk. Everything here is two years newer than the letter in your bag. You stand outside it in last night's clothes, and feel every one of those two years.
text.B2: The new development offers a glass lobby, lit and quite empty, a guard's cap abandoned on an untended desk. Everything in it is two full years newer than the letter folded in your bag. Standing outside it in last night's crumpled clothes, you feel the weight of every one of those years settle on you.

text.A2: Try the gate and the night watchman.
text.B1: Try the gate and the night watchman.
text.B2: Try the gate and the night watchman.

text.A2: Wait for morning by the quay.
text.B1: Wait for morning by the quay.
text.B2: Wait for morning by the quay.

text.A2: You wait for the café to open. The sky goes from black to grey. Your feet have stopped hurting, which may be worse. At last a light comes on inside. A chair scrapes.
text.B1: You wait for the café to open. The sky goes slowly from black to the colour of dishwater. Your feet have stopped hurting, which you suspect is worse than if they still did. At last a light comes on inside, and a chair scrapes.
text.B2: You wait for the café to open. The sky shades by slow degrees from black to the exact colour of dishwater. Your feet have stopped hurting, which you strongly suspect is a worse sign than if they still ached. At long last a light comes on inside, and somewhere a chair scrapes across a floor.

text.A2: Ask the counter man when they open properly.
text.B1: Ask the counter man when they open properly.
text.B2: Ask the counter man when they open properly.

text.A2: Wait at the window.
text.B1: Wait at the window.
text.B2: Wait at the window.

text.A2: An early customer looks up from his tea. "Kessler and Rowe? I did their books, years ago. Good people." He laughs. "Bad with letters, though. Always were. Ask anyone."
text.B1: One of the early regulars looks up from his tea. "Kessler and Rowe? I did their books, years back. Good people." He laughs at some private joke. "Bad with letters, mind. Always were. Ask anyone who ever waited on one."
text.B2: One of the early regulars glances up from his tea. "Kessler and Rowe? I kept their books, years back. Good people, the pair of them." He laughs at some joke of his own. "Hopeless with letters, mind — always were. Ask anyone who ever sat waiting on one to arrive."

text.A2: Head for the quay while there's time.
text.B1: Head for the quay while there's time.
text.B2: Head for the quay while there's time.
